references.text: Moses refers back to the Lord's earlier command to set boundaries around the mountain and consecrate it, which was given in these verses.
The Lord's repeated warning to Moses that the people must not break through to see the Lord, which forms the immediate context for Moses' response.
A similar prohibition against coming near Mount Sinai when the Lord reveals Himself, this time at the renewal of the covenant.
The book of Hebrews refers to the Sinai event and the terrifying fact that the people could not approach the mountain, as a contrast to the new covenant.
The concept of holy ground where Moses was told to take off his sandals at the burning bush, demonstrating God's holiness and the necessity of boundaries.
Direct narrative connection: Moses' ascent (v.3) is the reason for his warning about descending and setting boundaries (v.23).
Theological parallel: The fear of God's presence justifies both the setting of boundaries (v.23) and the people's desire for a mediator (v.19).
